analysis.one_liner: Moves large multistate consumer class action lawsuits out of state courts and into federal court.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 222-207 on September 23, 1999, but the Senate Judiciary Committee never acted, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would send most class actions where plaintiffs and defendants come from different states into federal court, and let a single defendant move a case there even if the case was filed in a state court. State courts are generally considered friendlier to consumers suing large companies; federal courts make it harder to form a class. The bill did not change the underlying law consumers sue under, only where the cases can be heard.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations facing consumer class actions — over products, fees, contracts, or services — would gain a route out of state courts. Federal judges apply stricter standards for certifying a class, so many cases would shrink to individual claims or be dismissed. Corporate defendants would face smaller, slower, and more scattered legal threats.

how_it_helps.text: The bill grants federal district courts jurisdiction over class actions in which any class member is from a different state than any defendant [S2][S5].

It lets any single defendant remove a class action to federal court without the consent of other defendants, and without regard to whether any defendant is a citizen of the state where the case was filed [S3][S4][S5].
Supporters argued interstate class actions implicate interstate commerce and attract local bias against businesses, so federal courts would adjudicate them more fairly and consistently [S5].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers who band together to sue a national company would bear the cost: their cases would move to federal court, where forming a class is harder, and cases that fail there could be refiled only to be removed again. Smaller recoveries and more litigation detours fall on the people the class action was designed to protect.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers suing companies over products and fees

drawbacks.text: The bill preserves state-court access only for narrow categories — cases where the claims fall under $1 million in the aggregate or fewer than 100 plaintiffs, purely intrastate cases, and cases against state governments; and it carves out securities and corporate-governance claims entirely [S3][S5].

Opponents argued the change would strip consumers of their local, accessible state courts and make it harder to hold national companies accountable; federal courts were also already carrying heavy caseloads, and the bill itself ordered a study of the impact on federal court workload [S3][S5].

The bill does not change the substantive rights consumers can enforce, only the forum — so a consumer who loses the venue fight still has a claim, but a weaker practical path to pursue it as a group [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated goal — consistent treatment of cases spanning many states — has some merit, but the bill's practical effect runs one way: it hands corporate defendants a tool to move consumer cases out of the courts where plaintiffs filed them and into a system where class certification is harder. The benefits flow mainly to repeat defendants; the costs fall on scattered class members with small individual claims, exactly the people least able to litigate alone.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 222-207, but after the Senate received it in September 1999 it sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee and never came to a vote before the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Goodlatte introduced the bill on May 19, 1999, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S1][S7].
The Judiciary Committee held hearings in July, amended the bill in markup, and reported it on September 14, 1999, having ordered it reported by a 15-12 vote [S7][S3].
The House passed the amended bill 222-207 on September 23, 1999 (Roll no. 443) [S8][S7].

The Senate received the bill on September 24, 1999, referred it to the Judiciary Committee on November 19, 1999, and took no further action before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S7][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and plaintiffs' lawyers, in the sense that the existing state-court route for class actions against national companies stayed open. Corporate defendants did not get the federal escape hatch, though the same fight would return in later Congresses.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers kept the state-court route to sue

sides.party_line_note: House passage split sharply by party: 204 of 221 Republicans voted yes while 191 of 211 Democrats voted no, and the bill's 37 cosponsors included 30 Republicans and 7 Democrats [S8][S6].

industries.industry: Corporate defendants in consumer class actions
industries.note: The bill gives any defendant a one-way door out of state court, where consumer classes are more easily certified, and into federal court, where they are harder to form. The industry's gain is the reduced legal exposure of exactly the cases ordinary consumers bring.

Fewer cases would survive federal class certification, shrinking the contingency-fee model that finances most consumer class litigation. Their interest in this bill ran alongside their clients' access to group lawsuits.

The bill would shift a large volume of cases into federal dockets already described as congested, which is why it ordered a Comptroller General study of the workload impact. More federal cases, fewer state cases.
